result:
Solution 1 is correct, assuming the intended model is that every layer spans the same total width, so bricks in different layers have different widths.

Take layer n to have M = 2ⁿ − 1 bricks, so layer n+1 has 2M + 1 bricks. Brick k in layer n covers [(k−1)/M, k/M], and brick j in layer n+1 covers [(j−1)/(2M+1), j/(2M+1)]. Two bricks in adjacent layers share a side when these intervals overlap in positive length.

The overlap conditions are j < k(2M+1)/M + 1 and j > (k−1)(2M+1)/M. Writing (2M+1)/M = 2 + 1/M turns these into:

- j < 2k + 1 + k/M, so j ≤ 2k + 1 (this also holds at k = M, where it gives j ≤ 2M + 1).
- j > 2k − 2 + (k−1)/M, so j ≥ 2k − 1 (this also holds at k = 1, where it gives j ≥ 1).

So every brick k touches exactly bricks 2k−1, 2k and 2k+1 below it, and all three exist: 1 ≤ 2k−1 and 2k+1 ≤ 2M+1. As a check, in layer 2 (M = 3), brick 2 spans [1/3, 2/3] and touches exactly bricks 3, 4 and 5 of the 7 in layer 3.

Jessica therefore has 3 independent choices at each of her 2025 moves. Different choice sequences give different brick sequences, so the total is 3²⁰²⁵.

If all bricks had the same width and the layers were centered, the layers would line up exactly, and Jessica would have only one move at each step. That reading makes the problem trivial, so I did not take it as the intended one.

Solutions 2 and 3 assume a half-brick offset between layers, which does not fit the brick counts 2ⁿ − 1, so their answers (2²⁰²⁵ and C(2025, 1012)) are wrong.

CHOICE: 1
